tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: TaskCreate
tools.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

description.description: What needs to be done

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

tools.name: TaskUpdate
tools.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

taskId.description: The ID of the task to update

subject.description: New subject for the task

description.description: New description for the task

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

addBlocks.description: Task IDs that this task blocks

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

metadata.description: Metadata keys to merge into the task. Set a key to null to delete it.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. """Reading the order book."""
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal
from pathlib import Path

DEFAULT_PATH = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data" / "orders.json"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Order:
    id: int
    customer: str
    total: Decimal
    placed_on: date


def load_orders(path: Path = DEFAULT_PATH) -> list[Order]:
    """Every order in the book, oldest first."""
    raw = json.loads(Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    orders = [
        Order(
            id=item["id"],
            customer=item["customer"],
            total=Decimal(item["total"]),
            placed_on=date.fromisoformat(item["placed_on"]),
        )
        for item in raw
    ]
    return sorted(orders, key=lambda o: (o.placed_on, o.id))

import json
import tempfile
import unittest
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal
from pathlib import Path

from orders.store import load_orders


class LoadOrdersTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_orders_are_sorted_oldest_first(self):
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
            path = Path(tmp) / "orders.json"
            path.write_text(json.dumps([
                {"id": 2, "customer": "B", "total": "5.00", "placed_on": "2026-03-02"},
                {"id": 1, "customer": "A", "total": "7.50", "placed_on": "2026-03-01"},
            ]))
            orders = load_orders(path)
        self.assertEqual([o.id for o in orders], [1, 2])
        self.assertEqual(orders[0].total, Decimal("7.50"))
        self.assertEqual(orders[0].placed_on, date(2026, 3, 1))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

entries.name: TaskCreate
entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

description.description: What needs to be done

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

entries.name: TaskUpdate
entries.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

taskId.description: The ID of the task to update

subject.description: New subject for the task

description.description: New description for the task

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

addBlocks.description: Task IDs that this task blocks

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

metadata.description: Metadata keys to merge into the task. Set a key to null to delete it.

"""Command line for the order book."""
import argparse

from orders.store import load_orders


def main(argv=None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="orders")

"""Reading the order book."""
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal
from pathlib import Path

DEFAULT_PATH = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data" / "orders.json"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Order:
    id: int
    customer: str
    total: Decimal
    placed_on: date


def load_orders(path: Path = DEFAULT_PATH) -> list[Order]:
    """Every order in the book, oldest first."""
    raw = json.loads(Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    orders = [
        Order(
            id=item["id"],
            customer=item["customer"],
            total=Decimal(item["total"]),
            placed_on=date.fromisoformat(item["placed_on"]),
        )
        for item in raw
    ]
    return sorted(orders, key=lambda o: (o.placed_on, o.id))

import unittest
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal
from pathlib import Path

from orders.store import load_orders


class LoadOrdersTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_orders_are_sorted_oldest_first(self):
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
            path = Path(tmp) / "orders.json"
            path.write_text(json.dumps([
                {"id": 2, "customer": "B", "total": "5.00", "placed_on": "2026-03-02"},
                {"id": 1, "customer": "A", "total": "7.50", "placed_on": "2026-03-01"},
            ]))
            orders = load_orders(path)
        self.assertEqual([o.id for o in orders], [1, 2])
        self.assertEqual(orders[0].total, Decimal("7.50"))
        self.assertEqual(orders[0].placed_on, date(2026, 3, 1))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

# ordersdesk

A small order book for the shop's back office.

```sh
python3 -m orders list            # print every order
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests
```

Orders live in `data/orders.json`.
=== data/orders.json

  {"id": 1001, "customer": "Lindqvist Bygg AB", "total": "1250.00", "placed_on": "2026-09-01"},
  {"id": 1002, "customer": "Norrlands Café", "total": "89.50", "placed_on": "2026-09-03"},
  {"id": 1003, "customer": "Åkesson & Dotter", "total": "432.10", "placed_on": "2026-09-03"},
  {"id": 1004, "customer": "Berg, Hanna", "total": "15.00", "placed_on": "2026-09-08"},
  {"id": 1005, "customer": "Sjöberg Trading", "total": "2999.99", "placed_on": "2026-09-12"}
]
=== orders/__init__.py
=== orders/__main__.py
"""Command line for the order book."""
import argparse

from orders.store import load_orders


def main(argv=None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="orders")
    commands = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)
    commands.add_parser("list", help="print every order")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    if args.command == "list":
        for order in load_orders():
            print(f"{order.id:>4}  {order.placed_on}  {order.customer:<24} {order.total:>10}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
=== orders/store.py
"""Reading the order book."""
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal
from pathlib import Path

DEFAULT_PATH = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data" / "orders.json"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Order:
    id: int
    customer: str
    total: Decimal
    placed_on: date


def load_orders(path: Path = DEFAULT_PATH) -> list[Order]:
    """Every order in the book, oldest first."""
    raw = json.loads(Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    orders = [
        Order(
            id=item["id"],
            customer=item["customer"],
            total=Decimal(item["total"]),
            placed_on=date.fromisoformat(item["placed_on"]),
        )
        for item in raw
    ]
    return sorted(orders, key=lambda o: (o.placed_on, o.id))

import tempfile
import unittest
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal
from pathlib import Path

from orders.store import load_orders


class LoadOrdersTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_orders_are_sorted_oldest_first(self):
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
            path = Path(tmp) / "orders.json"
            path.write_text(json.dumps([
                {"id": 2, "customer": "B", "total": "5.00", "placed_on": "2026-03-02"},
                {"id": 1, "customer": "A", "total": "7.50", "placed_on": "2026-03-01"},
            ]))
            orders = load_orders(path)
        self.assertEqual([o.id for o in orders], [1, 2])
        self.assertEqual(orders[0].total, Decimal("7.50"))
        self.assertEqual(orders[0].placed_on, date(2026, 3, 1))


if __name__ == "__main__":

Write the durable artifacts alongside it; write the feature's brief where the project's conventions say the build reads it (see *Which artifacts this design needs*).
8	
9	If the scans found nothing and no documentation directory is obvious, ask. Once, in one line, **with a concrete suggestion** — one that fits what the repo actually looks like, its ecosystem's convention or a `docs/` that already exists, rather than a preference of your own. Use the answer for everything in this capture.
10	
11	Ask at most once per project. After this, the files exist and Phase 2's scan finds them, so the destination is derived rather than asked.
12	
13	Keep the artifacts together, and keep their names recognizable, because the next interview's scan has to find them.
14	
15	## Provenance
16	
17	Artifacts need detail the design tree does not always carry. The tree records decisions; a functional spec records behavior, a data model records constraints, acceptance criteria record cases. Some of that was decided in the interview. Some of it will be you filling gaps.
18	
19	Both are acceptable. Only one is acceptable *silently*.
20	
21	- A statement tracing to a branch closed **decided** is written plainly.
22	- A statement you inferred is **marked as inference, inline, with what it was inferred from.** Not collected in a footnote at the end where it reads as afterthought.
23	- A statement that would resolve a branch closed **deferred**, **blocked**, or **stable-open** is not written at all. Those are open on purpose, and quietly closing one in prose destroys the reason they were left open.
24	
25	Never let the two look alike. A document where agreed decisions and plausible invention are typographically identical gets implemented as though all of it was agreed.
26	
27	## Capture is a completeness check
28	
29	Anything an artifact needs that the tree doesn't have is a gap in the interview, not a gap in your writing. Treat it that way.
30	
31	When a section can't be written from decided branches:
32	
33	1. Name the branches that are missing, or that closed too loosely to write from.
34	2. Offer to reopen them. This is a normal continuation of Phase 5 and the four locks still apply.
35	3. Write the section on marked inference only if the user declines.
36	
37	Reaching the end of capture with no gaps to report is real evidence the interview was thorough. Reaching it having invented a third of the content and said nothing is the failure this phase exists to prevent. **Report the gap count even when it is zero.**
38	
39	## Vocabulary
40	
41	Every artifact uses the lexicon, and only the lexicon, for anything the lexicon names. Artifacts diverging on terminology is the specific failure the lexicon exists to prevent, and it shows up here first — the data model calling something a `member` while the contract calls it a `user` is how two correct-looking documents produce two different systems.
42	
43	A term the artifacts need that isn't in the lexicon is a gap like any other. Surface it; don't quietly coin one.
44	
45	**Write the lexicon back.** Whenever capture runs, the consolidated lexicon is written back to where it was ingested from, or to the destination established above if there wasn't one. This is unconditional and it is not optional: the artifacts are written in this vocabulary, so a reader without the lexicon has documents whose terms mean whatever they assume. It is also what the next interview ingests. Show which entries are new and which changed before writing. An inherited entry changes only where this design changed what the word means.
46	
47	## Assumptions and tracker candidates
48	
49	**Write the assumptions record back**, to where it was ingested from, or to the destination established above. Unconditional, like the lexicon, and for the same reason: it is not a deliverable, it is what the next interview reads, and what a review of the build checks its platform assumptions against.
50	
51	It holds the assumptions still standing, each with a stable id, the assumption in one line, the subject area, and **how you would know it stopped holding** — an assumption recorded without that is decoration; with it, a later interview can actually check — plus the facts the project has measured that would cost time to rediscover. Remove an assumption the interview invalidated rather than annotating it; if the resolution was a real fork it became an ADR, and that is where the history belongs.
52	
53	**Branches closed *deferred-later*, *blocked*, or *stable-open* are not written to a file.** They are the next design questions, and a file of them turns into a backlog the tracker already is. Emit them as tracker candidates: one line each with the question, why it is open, and **what would resolve it**, for the user to file. The next interview asks which tracker items touch its work.
54	
55	## Which artifacts this design needs
56	
57	**Two outlive the feature: the decision records and the lexicon** (and the assumptions record, above). They are kept in the tree and kept true. Everything else in the tables below is **the feature's brief**: it tells the build and its reviewers what was decided, in the detail the tree does not carry, and it is spent when the feature ships — the code is its own domain model and interface contract, the tests carry the criteria, the project's references carry the behaviour. Write the brief where the project's conventions say the build reads it: on the tracker issue when the project works from one, else in the documentation directory marked as a brief. Do not carry a brief into the next interview as if it described the system; scan the code and the durable three instead.
58	
59	Four are unconditional:
60	
61	| Artifact | Template |
62	|---|---|
63	| Decision records (ADRs) | the `design:adr` skill — see below |
64	| Functional specification | `artifacts/functional-spec.md` |
65	| Edge cases and error handling | `artifacts/edge-cases.md` |
66	| Acceptance criteria | `artifacts/acceptance-criteria.md` |
67	
68	The rest are selected by the same conditions check that seeded the tree (`conditions-and-patterns.md`). If the condition held at seeding, the artifact is required now:
69	
70	| Artifact | Required when | Template |
71	|---|---|---|
72	| Interface / contract definitions | *Callers you can't change in lockstep*, or any boundary between components that ship or evolve separately | `artifacts/interface-contract.md` |
73	| Domain model | *The same concept has more than one shape*, *state outlives a single version*, *holds data that belongs to someone else* | `artifacts/domain-model.md` |
74	| Non-functional requirements | *It runs inside a constrained envelope*, *someone operates it in production* | not yet templated |
75	
76	There is deliberately no state-machine artifact. State and lifecycle content is unconditional and lives in the functional spec, which already requires every state, every transition, and every terminal state. A separate artifact would reformat content another artifact owns — a pass-through layer. Where a lifecycle is complex enough to need a diagram, the spec renders it as one.
77	
78	### Decision records
79	
80	**Every ADR-worthy decision gets an ADR, always.** Not conditional, not on request, not deferred to the user's judgment at write-up time. Invoke the `design:adr` skill and let it write them — it owns format, house rules, numbering, indexing, and supersession, and none of that is reimplemented here.
81	
82	A branch that closed *decided* is ADR-worthy when a real fork existed and the decision passes the `design:adr` skill's tests for what gets an ADR. A real fork means the closure recorded it as one, with the alternatives and why each was rejected. Read that line; don't reconstruct it from the rationale. A closure recorded as *no fork* is not an ADR no matter how consequential it feels — nothing was chosen.
83	
84	Not ADR-worthy: decisions with only one option ever available, choices forced by an existing constraint, anything the design-vs-implementation gate would have deferred, and anything an indexed ADR already covers.
85	
86	Two cases need care:
87	
88	- **A decision that contradicts an ADR indexed in Phase 2** is a supersession, not a new record. Say so and hand the `design:adr` skill both — it owns what happens next.
89	- **A branch that closed *stable-open* or *blocked*** is not a decision and gets no ADR. Leave it in the tree where its openness is visible.
90	
91	Give the `design:adr` skill, per decision: the question, the options considered **and why each was rejected**, the chosen path, the rationale from the closure, and any ADR it supersedes. The rejection reasons are not optional padding — they are what makes the record load-bearing later, when someone is weighing the same option again and needs to know it was already ruled out and on what grounds. Then let it work.
92	
93	For an artifact marked *not yet templated*, write it from the general rules on this page: provenance, lexicon discipline, and a stated completeness test of your own before you start.
94	
95	## Common shape
96	
97	Every artifact opens with the same three lines, because a reader needs them before the content:
98	
99	- **Sourced from:** the design tree of [date/topic], N branches decided.
100	- **Gaps:** what could not be written from decided branches, or "none".
101	- **Inference:** how much of this document is marked inference, in one sentence.
102	
103	Then the artifact's own content. No preamble, no restating the pitch, no summary of the interview. The reader wants the design, not its history.
104

# Output Artifacts

Read this at Phase 9, before writing anything.

## Where artifacts go

**Nothing here has a hardcoded path.** The destination comes from the project, and Phase 2 already worked it out: whatever its scans found — ADRs, a lexicon, an assumptions record — establishes where this project keeps design documentation. Write the durable artifacts alongside it; write the feature's brief where the project's conventions say the build reads it (see *Which artifacts this design needs*).

If the scans found nothing and no documentation directory is obvious, ask. Once, in one line, **with a concrete suggestion** — one that fits what the repo actually looks like, its ecosystem's convention or a `docs/` that already exists, rather than a preference of your own. Use the answer for everything in this capture.

Ask at most once per project. After this, the files exist and Phase 2's scan finds them, so the destination is derived rather than asked.

Keep the artifacts together, and keep their names recognizable, because the next interview's scan has to find them.

## Provenance

Artifacts need detail the design tree does not always carry. The tree records decisions; a functional spec records behavior, a data model records constraints, acceptance criteria record cases. Some of that was decided in the interview. Some of it will be you filling gaps.

Both are acceptable. Only one is acceptable *silently*.

- A statement tracing to a branch closed **decided** is written plainly.
- A statement you inferred is **marked as inference, inline, with what it was inferred from.** Not collected in a footnote at the end where it reads as afterthought.
- A statement that would resolve a branch closed **deferred**, **blocked**, or **stable-open** is not written at all. Those are open on purpose, and quietly closing one in prose destroys the reason they were left open.

Never let the two look alike. A document where agreed decisions and plausible invention are typographically identical gets implemented as though all of it was agreed.

## Capture is a completeness check

Anything an artifact needs that the tree doesn't have is a gap in the interview, not a gap in your writing. Treat it that way.

When a section can't be written from decided branches:

1. Name the branches that are missing, or that closed too loosely to write from.
2. Offer to reopen them. This is a normal continuation of Phase 5 and the four locks still apply.
3. Write the section on marked inference only if the user declines.

Reaching the end of capture with no gaps to report is real evidence the interview was thorough. Reaching it having invented a third of the content and said nothing is the failure this phase exists to prevent. **Report the gap count even when it is zero.**

## Vocabulary

Every artifact uses the lexicon, and only the lexicon, for anything the lexicon names. Artifacts diverging on terminology is the specific failure the lexicon exists to prevent, and it shows up here first — the data model calling something a `member` while the contract calls it a `user` is how two correct-looking documents produce two different systems.

A term the artifacts need that isn't in the lexicon is a gap like any other. Surface it; don't quietly coin one.

**Write the lexicon back.** Whenever capture runs, the consolidated lexicon is written back to where it was ingested from, or to the destination established above if there wasn't one. This is unconditional and it is not optional: the artifacts are written in this vocabulary, so a reader without the lexicon has documents whose terms mean whatever they assume. It is also what the next interview ingests. Show which entries are new and which changed before writing. An inherited entry changes only where this design changed what the word means.

## Assumptions and tracker candidates

**Write the assumptions record back**, to where it was ingested from, or to the destination established above. Unconditional, like the lexicon, and for the same reason: it is not a deliverable, it is what the next interview reads, and what a review of the build checks its platform assumptions against.

It holds the assumptions still standing, each with a stable id, the assumption in one line, the subject area, and **how you would know it stopped holding** — an assumption recorded without that is decoration; with it, a later interview can actually check — plus the facts the project has measured that would cost time to rediscover. Remove an assumption the interview invalidated rather than annotating it; if the resolution was a real fork it became an ADR, and that is where the history belongs.

**Branches closed *deferred-later*, *blocked*, or *stable-open* are not written to a file.** They are the next design questions, and a file of them turns into a backlog the tracker already is. Emit them as tracker candidates: one line each with the question, why it is open, and **what would resolve it**, for the user to file. The next interview asks which tracker items touch its work.

# Plan — order book on SQLite

## 1. Design
Assumptions
- A1 — `sqlite3` from the standard library is enough. Stops holding when: a query needs a feature it lacks.

Branches
1. Scope — decided (requester). Orders live in `data/orders.db`; `data/orders.json` is migrated once and then removed. Non-goals: new commands, a server database. Only this repo reads the JSON (requester).
2. Store interface — decided (requester). `orders.store.load_orders(path: Path = DEFAULT_PATH) -> list[Order]` keeps its signature; only its implementation (and DEFAULT_PATH's value) changes. Fork: callers query SQL directly — rejected, every caller would learn the schema.
3. Schema — decided (requester). One `orders` table: `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT, total TEXT, placed_on TEXT`; totals as text so `89.50` keeps two places.
4. Migration — decided (requester). One-shot `python3 -m orders migrate` reads the JSON and writes the database; refuses to run twice.
   4a. How "twice" is detected — suggestion (me): the database file already exists → refuse, exit 1, file untouched.
   4b. Atomicity — suggestion (me): migration writes to a temporary file beside the target and renames it into place, so a failed run leaves no database and can be retried.
   4c. Who removes the JSON — suggestion (me): the migrate command does not delete it; the cutover commit runs the migration, commits `data/orders.db` and `git rm`s `data/orders.json`. Keeps the command non-destructive.
   4d. Where the code lives — suggestion (me): schema and the writer in `orders/store.py` (store owns the schema); JSON parsing in `orders/migrate.py`, which only `migrate` imports. After cutover nothing on the read path touches JSON.
5. What must not change — decided (requester). `orders list` output stays byte-identical; the existing tests keep passing.
   5a. Conflict — suggestion (me): the existing test `test_orders_are_sorted_oldest_first` builds a JSON file and passes it to `load_orders`; under [2] it cannot pass unchanged. Amend [5] to "the existing test's assertions (sort order oldest first, `Decimal` total, `date` placed_on) keep passing, with its fixture rebuilt as a temporary database per [6]". Those assertions become criterion AC1, not a guardrail, since they cannot pass at base with a DB fixture.
6. Testing — decided (requester). `unittest`, against a temporary database.
7. The database in git — suggestion (me): `data/orders.db` is committed, as `data/orders.json` was; it is the order book and removing the JSON would otherwise drop the data from the repo.
8. Missing database — suggestion (me): `load_orders` opens read-only (`file:...?mode=ro`) and raises `FileNotFoundError` when the file is absent, as the JSON read did, instead of sqlite silently creating an empty file.
9. Docs location — suggestion (me), to confirm: ADRs in `docs/adr/`, assumptions in `docs/assumptions.md`; brief lives in this plan and the PR bodies (no tracker).

Lexicon delta: none (no lexicon exists; no new terms).

## 2. Brief
Sourced from: the design tree of 2026-10-20, order book on SQLite; 6 branches decided by the requester, 3 sub-branches and 3 branches (7–9) suggested by me. Gaps: 5a, 7, 8, 9 need the requester's yes. Inference: everything tagged "suggestion" above.

### Functional spec
- F1 [1][2] `load_orders()` reads every order from `data/orders.db` and returns them sorted by (`placed_on`, `id`), `total` as `Decimal`, `placed_on` as `date`.
- F2 [4][4a][4b] `python3 -m orders migrate` reads `data/orders.json`, writes `data/orders.db` with the [3] schema, prints `migrated N orders`, exits 0. If the db exists, prints an error to stderr and exits 1 without touching it.
- F3 [1][4c][7] After cutover the repo contains `data/orders.db` with the five orders and no `data/orders.json`; README says orders live in `data/orders.db` and documents `migrate`.

### Acceptance criteria (check)
- AC1 [2][5a][6] load_orders on a temp DB: sorted oldest first, Decimal total, date placed_on — `python3 -m unittest tests.test_store.LoadOrdersTest.test_orders_are_sorted_oldest_first`
- AC2 [4][3] migrate writes every JSON order into the `orders` table with the [3] columns — `python3 -m unittest tests.test_migrate.MigrateTest.test_writes_every_order`
- AC3 [3] schema is exactly one table `orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT, total TEXT, placed_on TEXT)` — `python3 -m unittest tests.test_migrate.MigrateTest.test_schema`
- AC4 [1][7] the repo's `data/orders.db` holds orders 1001–1005 and `data/orders.json` is gone — `python3 -m unittest tests.test_cutover.CutoverTest.test_book_is_in_database`
- AC5 [1][2] `orders list` works with no JSON on disk (copy of the repo, JSON deleted) and matches the golden output — `python3 -m unittest tests.test_cutover.CutoverTest.test_list_reads_database_only`
- AC6 [1] README names `data/orders.db` and `migrate`, not `orders.json` as the store — judged
- AC7 [4] `python3 -m orders migrate` CLI runs the migration against its default paths (paths patched in test) and exits 0 — `python3 -m unittest tests.test_migrate.MigrateTest.test_cli_migrate`

- E1 [4][4a] DB already exists → exit 1, stderr message, file bytes unchanged — `python3 -m unittest tests.test_migrate.MigrateTest.test_refuses_second_run`

## 3. Slices — horizontal
Storage swap: a per-feature vertical cut would leave readers split across two stores. Cut horizontally: the write path first, then the read-path cutover.
| Slice | Repo | Base | Direction | PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 `orders-db-migrate` | ordersdesk | main | Add schema + writer to store, `orders/migrate.py`, `migrate` command; readers still on JSON. AC2, AC3, AC7, E1–E4; G1–G3 | PR 1 |
| S2 `orders-db-cutover` | ordersdesk | S1 | `load_orders` reads SQLite read-only; run migration, commit `data/orders.db`, remove JSON, rebuild the existing test on a DB, README. AC1, AC4, AC5, AC6, E5; G1–G3 | PR 2 (stacked) |
Each leaves the system consistent: after S1 the JSON is still the single source; after S2 the DB is.

## 4. Capture (first commit)
- ADR-0001 [1][2][3] Store the order book in SQLite behind `load_orders` (alternatives: keep JSON; callers query SQL directly; numeric/REAL totals).

- Lexicon: none.
- Assumptions: add A1 to `docs/assumptions.md` [1].

## 5. Progress

# Plan: order book to SQLite

## 1. Design

**Assumptions**
- A1: `sqlite3` from the standard library is enough. Stops holding when a query needs a feature it lacks.

**Branches**
1. **Scope** (decided, requester). Orders live in `data/orders.db`; `data/orders.json` is migrated once and then removed. Nothing outside this repo reads it (requester). Non-goals: new commands beyond `migrate`, a server database.
2. **Store interface** (decided, requester). `orders.store.load_orders(path)` keeps its signature; only its implementation changes. Rejected: callers query SQL directly. Sub-choice (suggestion, mine): it opens the database read-only (`file:…?mode=ro`), so a missing database raises an error instead of sqlite silently creating an empty file.
3. **Schema** (decided, requester). One `orders` table: `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT, total TEXT, placed_on TEXT`; totals stored as text so `89.50` keeps two places.
4. **Migration** (decided, requester). One-shot `python3 -m orders migrate` reads the JSON and writes the database, and refuses to run if the database already exists. Sub-choices (suggestion, mine): the logic lives in `orders.store.migrate(source, target)` and the CLI calls it with the default paths; it writes to a temporary file and renames it into place, so a failed run leaves no database behind.
5. **What must not change** (decided, requester). `orders list` output stays byte-identical; the existing tests keep passing. **Conflict:** `tests/test_store.py` builds a JSON fixture, so it can't pass once `load_orders` reads SQLite. Proposed amendment (suggestion, mine): the fixture moves to SQLite and the test's three assertions stay word for word; the guardrail becomes "the full suite passes at base and at head" plus a judged check that those assertions survive.
6. **Testing** (decided, requester). `unittest`, against a temporary database.
7. **Tracking** (new, suggestion, mine). `data/orders.db` is committed, as `data/orders.json` was, and is produced by running `migrate` on the real JSON. `README.md` says orders live in `data/orders.db`.

**Lexicon delta:** none (the repo has no lexicon; none is created).

## 2. Brief

**Functional spec.** `load_orders(path=DEFAULT_PATH)` reads every row of the `orders` table in the SQLite database at `path` (default `data/orders.db`) and returns `Order`s oldest first, ties broken by id. `python3 -m orders migrate` copies `data/orders.json` into a new `data/orders.db`. `orders list` behaves as before.

- AC4 [1][7]: at HEAD, `data/orders.json` is gone and `data/orders.db` holds 5 orders. Check: `test ! -e data/orders.json && python3 -c "import sqlite3; assert sqlite3.connect('file:data/orders.db?mode=ro', uri=True).execute('select count(*) from orders').fetchone()[0] == 5"`
- AC5 [1][7]: no code or docs point at `orders.json`, except migration code. Check: `! grep -rn "orders.json" orders/__main__.py README.md && grep -q "data/orders.db" README.md`

# Plan — order book on SQLite

Repo: ordersdesk (this checkout), base `main` @ ea4086f.

## 1. Design

**Assumptions**
- A1 — `sqlite3` from the standard library is enough. Stops holding when: a query needs a feature it lacks.

**Branches** (closed by the requester unless marked *suggestion*)
1. **Scope** — decided. Orders live in `data/orders.db`; `data/orders.json` is migrated once and then removed. Non-goals: new commands (beyond `migrate`), a server database. Nothing outside this repo reads `data/orders.json` (requester).
2. **Store interface** — decided. `orders.store.load_orders()` keeps its signature; only its implementation changes. Fork: callers query SQL directly — rejected, every caller would learn the schema.
3. **Schema** — decided. One `orders` table: `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT, total TEXT, placed_on TEXT`; totals as text so `89.50` keeps two places.
4. **Migration** — decided. One-shot `python3 -m orders migrate` reads the JSON and writes the database; refuses to run twice.
5. **What must not change** — decided. `orders list` output stays byte-identical; the existing tests keep passing.
6. **Testing** — decided. `unittest`, against a temporary database.
7. **Migration mechanics** — *suggestion (me)*. "Twice" means `data/orders.db` already exists: `migrate` then exits 1 with a one-line message on stderr and leaves the database untouched. `migrate` never deletes the JSON. It writes to a temporary file beside the target and renames it into place only after every row is in, so a failed run (JSON missing, malformed, duplicate id) leaves no `orders.db` behind. Paths are parameters of `orders.store.migrate(json_path, db_path)`; the CLI passes the defaults. No CLI flags.
8. **Who runs the migration** — *suggestion (me)*. This PR runs `migrate` once on the repo's own `data/orders.json`, commits the resulting `data/orders.db`, and deletes `data/orders.json` with `git rm`. The command stays for any checkout whose JSON is ahead of the repo.
9. **Missing database** — *suggestion (me)*. `load_orders(path)` on a path that doesn't exist raises `FileNotFoundError` and creates no file (today's behaviour for a missing JSON; plain `sqlite3.connect` would silently create an empty file).
10. **Existing test's fixture** — *suggestion (me), resolves a conflict between [2] and [5]*. `tests/test_store.py` writes a JSON fixture and passes its path to `load_orders`; once `load_orders` reads SQLite, that fixture cannot pass. Its assertions (oldest-first, `Decimal` total, `date` placed_on) are kept verbatim; only its fixture becomes a temporary database.

**Lexicon delta:** none. **Counts:** 10 closed (6 by requester, 4 suggestions), 0 open.

## 2. Brief

**Sourced from:** the design tree of 2026-10-20, order book on SQLite, 10 branches closed. **Gaps:** none after [7]–[10]. **Inference:** [7]–[10] are my suggestions, marked.

### Functional spec
- **Reading** [2][3]: `load_orders(path=DEFAULT_PATH)` opens the SQLite database at `path` (default `data/orders.db`), reads every row of `orders`, returns `list[Order]` sorted by `(placed_on, id)`. `total` → `Decimal(text)`, `placed_on` → `date.fromisoformat(text)`. Missing path → `FileNotFoundError`, no file created [9].
- **Listing** [5]: `python3 -m orders list` prints exactly what it printed from JSON.
- **Migrating** [4][7]: `python3 -m orders migrate` → `store.migrate(data/orders.json, data/orders.db)`. Precondition: db absent. Creates the `orders` table [3], inserts every JSON item with `total` and `placed_on` stored as the JSON's text verbatim, renames into place, prints `migrated N orders to data/orders.db`, exits 0. Precondition fails → stderr `orders: data/orders.db already exists; migrate runs once`, exit 1, db untouched.
- **Data** [1][8]: repo ships `data/orders.db` with the five orders; `data/orders.json` is gone; README says orders live in `data/orders.db`.
- Non-goals [1]: other new commands, server database, concurrent `migrate` runs (one operator, one shot — two simultaneous runs is unspecified).

### Edge cases
- E1 [7] JSON missing → `migrate` exits 1, stderr names the path, no db created.
- E2 [7] JSON malformed (not valid JSON) → exit 1, no db created, no temp file left.
- E3 [3][7] duplicate `id` in JSON → exit 1 (PRIMARY KEY), no db created.
- E4 [2] empty order book (`[]`) → db with zero rows; `load_orders` returns `[]`.
- E5 [3] non-ASCII customer (`Åkesson & Dotter`) and trailing-zero total (`15.00`) round-trip JSON → db → `Order` unchanged.

### Acceptance criteria — check
- AC1 [2] Given a temporary database with rows inserted by plain `sqlite3`, `load_orders(path)` returns them as `Order`s, oldest first. — `python3 -m unittest tests.test_sqlite_store`
- AC2 [1][8] `data/orders.json` absent; `data/orders.db` holds exactly ids 1001–1005. — `python3 -m unittest tests.test_order_book`
- AC3 [3] A total stored as `89.50` reads back as `Decimal('89.50')`, `str` = `89.50`. — `tests.test_sqlite_store`
- AC4 [3] `data/orders.db`'s `orders` table has columns `id INTEGER pk, customer TEXT, total TEXT, placed_on TEXT`. — `tests.test_order_book`
- AC5 [4][7] `migrate(json, db)` on a fresh db writes every JSON item; `main(["migrate"])` path prints `migrated N orders …`. — `python3 -m unittest tests.test_migrate`
- AC6 [4][7] Second `migrate` → exit 1, stderr message, db bytes unchanged. — `tests.test_migrate`
- AC7 [1] README says `data/orders.db`, no longer `data/orders.json`. — `grep -q 'data/orders.db' README.md && ! grep -q 'data/orders.json' README.md`
- E1–E3 → `tests.test_migrate`; E4 → `tests.test_sqlite_store`; E5 → `tests.test_migrate`.

### Guardrails — check (must pass at base and HEAD)
- G1 [5] `orders list` output byte-identical to base, captured now as `tests/golden/orders-list.txt`. — `python3 -m orders list | cmp - tests/golden/orders-list.txt`
- G2 [5][10] Existing assertions hold: oldest-first, `Decimal` total, `date` placed_on. — `python3 -m unittest tests.test_store` (at base: the original JSON-fixture file; at HEAD: same assertions, DB fixture — see [10])
- G3 [2] `load_orders` has one parameter `path` annotated `Path` with a default, returns `list[Order]`; `Order` fields are `id, customer, total, placed_on`. — `python3 -m unittest tests.test_store_interface`
- G4 [9] `load_orders` on a missing path raises `FileNotFoundError` and creates no file. — `tests.test_store_interface`

## 3. Slices

| Slice | Repo | Base | Direction | PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. order book on SQLite | ordersdesk | `main` @ ea4086f | one slice (horizontal) | `orders-sqlite` → `main` |

One slice: a storage swap. Shipping the reader without the data breaks `list`; shipping `migrate` alone ships a command whose output nothing reads.

## 4. Capture
- ADR-0001 [1][3] Store the order book in SQLite (`data/orders.db`), totals as text. Alternatives: keep JSON; server DB (non-goal).
- ADR-0002 [2] `load_orders` stays the only reader of order storage. Rejected: callers query SQL directly.
- Lexicon [—]: no change; no lexicon file created.
- Assumptions [—]: add A1 to a new `docs/assumptions.md`.
- Location: `docs/adr/` and `docs/assumptions.md` (no docs directory exists yet — suggestion).

## 5. Progress
- [x] Intake
- [x] Designing
- [ ] Planning
- [ ] Building slices
- [ ] Proving changes
- [ ] Shipping PRs

# Plan: order book to SQLite

## 1. Design

**Assumptions**
- A1: `sqlite3` from the standard library is enough. Stops holding when a query needs a feature it lacks.

**Branches**
1. **Scope** (decided, requester). Orders live in `data/orders.db`; `data/orders.json` is migrated once and then removed. Nothing outside this repo reads it (requester). Non-goals: new commands beyond `migrate`, a server database.
2. **Store interface** (decided, requester). `orders.store.load_orders(path)` keeps its signature; only its implementation changes. Rejected: callers query SQL directly. Sub-choice (suggestion, mine): it opens the database read-only (`file:…?mode=ro`), so a missing database raises an error instead of sqlite silently creating an empty file.
3. **Schema** (decided, requester). One `orders` table: `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT, total TEXT, placed_on TEXT`; totals stored as text so `89.50` keeps two places.
4. **Migration** (decided, requester). One-shot `python3 -m orders migrate` reads the JSON and writes the database, and refuses to run if the database already exists. Sub-choices (suggestion, mine): the logic lives in `orders.store.migrate(source, target)` and the CLI calls it with the default paths; it writes to a temporary file and renames it into place, so a failed run leaves no database behind.
5. **What must not change** (decided, requester). `orders list` output stays byte-identical; the existing tests keep passing. **Conflict:** `tests/test_store.py` builds a JSON fixture, so it can't pass once `load_orders` reads SQLite. Proposed amendment (suggestion, mine): the fixture moves to SQLite and the test's three assertions stay word for word; the guardrail becomes "the full suite passes at base and at head" plus a judged check that those assertions survive.
6. **Testing** (decided, requester). `unittest`, against a temporary database.
7. **Tracking** (new, suggestion, mine). `data/orders.db` is committed, as `data/orders.json` was, and is produced by running `migrate` on the real JSON. `README.md` says orders live in `data/orders.db`.

**Lexicon delta:** none (the repo has no lexicon; none is created).

## 2. Brief

**Functional spec.** `load_orders(path=DEFAULT_PATH)` reads every row of the `orders` table in the SQLite database at `path` (default `data/orders.db`) and returns `Order`s oldest first, ties broken by id. `python3 -m orders migrate` copies `data/orders.json` into a new `data/orders.db`. `orders list` behaves as before.

**Acceptance criteria**
- AC1 [2][3]: `load_orders(db)` returns the rows of a SQLite database sorted by (placed_on, id), with `total` as `Decimal` and `placed_on` as `date`. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_sqlite_store.LoadOrdersFromDatabaseTest`
- AC2 [4]: `migrate(json, db)` creates a database holding every JSON order with identical field values. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_sqlite_store.MigrateTest.test_copies_every_order`
- AC3 [4]: `python3 -m orders migrate` exists and writes the database at the default path. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_sqlite_store.MigrateTest.test_cli_migrate_uses_default_paths` (patches the default paths to a temporary directory)
- AC4 [1][7]: at HEAD, `data/orders.json` is gone and `data/orders.db` holds 5 orders. Check: `test ! -e data/orders.json && python3 -c "import sqlite3; assert sqlite3.connect('file:data/orders.db?mode=ro', uri=True).execute('select count(*) from orders').fetchone()[0] == 5"`
- AC5 [1][7]: no code or docs point at `orders.json`, except migration code. Check: `! grep -rn "orders.json" orders/__main__.py README.md && grep -q "data/orders.db" README.md`

**Edge cases**
- E1 [3]: a total of `"89.50"` comes back as `Decimal("89.50")`, not `89.5`. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_sqlite_store.LoadOrdersFromDatabaseTest.test_total_keeps_two_places`
- E2 [4]: `migrate` refuses when the target exists: it raises an error, the CLI exits non-zero, and the existing file is left byte for byte. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_sqlite_store.MigrateTest.test_refuses_when_database_exists`
- E3 [4]: a migration that fails (malformed JSON) leaves no database file. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_sqlite_store.MigrateTest.test_failed_migration_leaves_no_database`
- E4 [2]: `load_orders` on a missing database raises an error and creates no file. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_sqlite_store.LoadOrdersFromDatabaseTest.test_missing_database_is_not_created`
- E5 [3]: non-ASCII customer names (`Åkesson & Dotter`) round-trip. Check: covered by G1 on the real data, plus `…LoadOrdersFromDatabaseTest.test_unicode_customer`

**Guardrails**
- G1 [5]: `python3 -m orders list` output is byte-identical to base. Check: `checks/list_golden.sh`, which diffs the output against base's output captured verbatim in `checks/list_golden.txt`
- G2 [5]: the full suite passes. Check: `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` at base and at head (each with its own tests)
- G3 [5]: the assertions of `test_orders_are_sorted_oldest_first` survive unchanged. Check: judged (diff of that test)
- G4 [2]: the `Order` fields and `load_orders`'s parameter names are unchanged. Check: `python3 -c "import dataclasses, inspect; from orders.store import Order, load_orders; assert [f.name for f in dataclasses.fields(Order)] == ['id','customer','total','placed_on']; assert list(inspect.signature(load_orders).parameters) == ['path']"`
- G5 [A1]: no third-party imports. Check: `python3 -c "import ast,sys,pathlib; mods={a.name.split('.')[0] for p in pathlib.Path('orders').glob('*.py') for n in ast.walk(ast.parse(p.read_text())) for a in getattr(n,'names',[]) if isinstance(n,(ast.Import,))} | {n.module.split('.')[0] for p in pathlib.Path('orders').glob('*.py') for n in ast.walk(ast.parse(p.read_text())) if isinstance(n,ast.ImportFrom) and n.module}; assert mods <= set(sys.stdlib_module_names) | {'orders'}, mods"`

Mutants: G1 change `>10` to `>11` in the list format; G2 flip the sort key; G3 edit one assertion (judged, shown by diff); G4 rename `placed_on`; G5 add `import requests`.

## 3. Slices

| Slice | Repo | Base | Direction | PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. `orders-sqlite`: schema, `migrate`, `load_orders` on SQLite, migrated `data/orders.db`, JSON removed, README | ordersdesk | `main` @ ea4086f | horizontal (storage swap, one slice) | one ready PR into `main` |

One slice, because this is a storage swap: shipping the reader swap without the migrated database, or the migration without the reader swap, leaves the repo with two sources of truth or a reader with no data. The whole change is under ~150 lines.

## 4. Capture
- ADR-0001 "Order book in SQLite" [1][2][3][4]: SQLite through the standard library, text totals, one-shot migrate, A1 recorded as its assumption. First ADR, so `docs/adr/` and its index are created.
- Lexicon: no change [—].
- Assumptions: A1 added, recorded in ADR-0001 [A1].

## 5. Progress
- [x] Intake
- [x] Designing
- [ ] Planning
- [ ] Building slices
- [ ] Proving changes
- [ ] Shipping PRs

# Plan: order book on SQLite (revised after adversarial review)

## 1. Design

**Assumptions**
- A1 [1]: `sqlite3` from the standard library is enough. *Stops holding when:* a query needs a feature it lacks.
- A2 [1]: nothing outside this repo reads `data/orders.json` (requester). *Stops holding when:* another consumer of the file turns up.

**Branches** (R = closed by the requester, S = my suggestion, needs your yes)
1. **Scope** (R): Orders live in `data/orders.db`. `data/orders.json` is migrated once and then removed. Non-goals: a server database, and new commands other than `migrate` [4].
2. **Store interface** (R): `load_orders(path: Path = DEFAULT_PATH) -> list[Order]` keeps its signature and `Order` keeps its fields and types. Only the implementation and the default's value change. Rejected fork: callers query SQL directly.
3. **Schema** (R): `orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT, total TEXT, placed_on TEXT)`. Totals are stored as text.
4. **Migration** (R): One-shot `python3 -m orders migrate` that refuses to run twice.
   - 4a (S): "Twice" means the database file exists. Then it prints `error: data/orders.db already exists` to stderr, exits 1 and leaves the file untouched.
   - 4b (S): Atomic. It writes to a temp file beside the target, then `os.link(tmp, target)`, which fails if the target appeared meanwhile, then unlinks the temp file. Any failure leaves neither file. It prints an error to stderr and exits 1.
   - 4c (S): The command never deletes the JSON. The cutover commit runs it, commits the db and `git rm`s the JSON.
   - 4d (S): `orders/store.py` owns the schema and gains `DATABASE_PATH` and `write_orders(path, orders)`. `orders/migrate.py` holds `SOURCE_PATH` and the JSON parsing, and is imported lazily inside the `migrate` branch of `__main__`. Nothing on the read path imports `json`.
   - 4e (S): On success it prints `migrated N orders` and exits 0.
5. **What must not change** (R): `orders list` output stays byte-identical, and the existing tests keep passing.
   - 5a (S): Amendment needed. `test_orders_are_sorted_oldest_first` builds a JSON file, so it cannot pass once [2] holds. Proposal: in S1 it passes unchanged (guardrail). In S2 its fixture becomes a temporary database [6] and its assertions are kept (criterion).
6. **Testing** (R): `unittest`, against a temporary database.
7. **Database in git** (S): `data/orders.db` is committed, as the JSON was. In S1 it goes in `.gitignore`, so a trial `migrate` can't be committed by accident. S2 removes that line and commits the db.
8. **Missing database** (S): `load_orders` checks that the file exists and raises `FileNotFoundError` if not. It opens the file read-only (`Path.as_uri()?mode=ro`), so sqlite never creates an empty file.
9. **`migrate` after cutover** (S): Keep it. It is what [4] decided. After S2 it refuses cleanly because the db exists. The README documents it as the one-shot that was already run. Removing it is a follow-up.
10. **Docs location** (S): ADRs go in `docs/adr/`, assumptions in `docs/assumptions.md`. There is no tracker, so the brief lives in this plan and in the PR bodies.

**Lexicon delta:** none. There is no lexicon and no new domain terms.
**Counts:** 6 decided by the requester. 5 sub-branches (4a–4e) and 5 branches/amendments (5a, 7–10) are my suggestions.

## 2. Brief
- **Sourced from:** the design tree of 2026-10-20 (order book on SQLite), 6 branches decided.
- **Gaps:** 4a–4e, 5a, 7, 8, 9, 10 are suggestions awaiting your yes.
- **Inference:** every line tagged with a suggestion branch is inference from the code and branches [1]–[6].

- F2 [4][4a][4b][4e]: `migrate` copies `data/orders.json` into `data/orders.db` and behaves as 4a, 4b and 4e describe.
- F3 [1][7][9]: After cutover, git tracks `data/orders.db` (five orders) and no `data/orders.json`. The README names the db and describes `migrate` as a one-shot.

|---|---|---|---|---|

| E4 | S1 | [3] | `Åkesson & Dotter` and `Sjöberg Trading` round-trip | `…MigrateTest.test_non_ascii_customers` |

**Guardrails** (must pass at both base and head of the slices listed)

| id | slices | branch | guardrail | check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G1 | S1, S2 | [5] | `python3 -m orders list` output is byte-identical to `tests/fixtures/orders_list.txt`, captured at main | `tests.test_guardrails.GuardrailTest.test_list_output_unchanged` |
| G2 | S1, S2 | [2] | `load_orders` has exactly one parameter, `path: Path` with a default, and returns `list[Order]`; `Order` fields are `{id: int, customer: str, total: Decimal, placed_on: date}` | `…GuardrailTest.test_store_interface_unchanged` |
| G3 | S1, S2 | [1] | the set of subcommands ⊆ `{"list", "migrate"}` and contains `"list"` | `…GuardrailTest.test_only_known_commands` |
| G4 | S2 | [8] | `load_orders` on a missing path raises `FileNotFoundError` and creates no file | `…GuardrailTest.test_missing_store_raises` |
| G5 | S1 | [5] | the original `tests/test_store.py` passes unchanged | `python3 -m unittest tests.test_store` |

## 3. Slices: horizontal
This is a storage swap. A per-feature cut would leave readers split across two stores, so it is cut by layer: the write path first, then the read-path cutover.

| Slice | Repo | Base | Direction | PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 `orders-db-migrate` | ordersdesk | `main` | schema + `write_orders` + `DATABASE_PATH` in store, `orders/migrate.py`, `migrate` command, `.gitignore` the db; readers still on JSON | PR 1 → main |

- Lexicon: no change.

- [x] Designing
- [ ] Planning
- [ ] Building slices
- [ ] Proving changes
- [ ] Shipping PRs

# Plan — order book on SQLite

Repo: ordersdesk (this checkout), base `main` @ ea4086f.

## 1. Design

**Assumptions**
- A1 [3] — `sqlite3` from the standard library (SQLite 3.53.4 here) is enough. Stops holding when: a query needs a feature it lacks.

**Branches** (closed by the requester unless marked *suggestion*)
1. **Scope** — decided. Orders live in `data/orders.db`; `data/orders.json` is migrated once, then removed. Non-goals: other new commands, a server database. Nothing outside this repo reads `data/orders.json` (requester).
2. **Store interface** — decided. `orders.store.load_orders()` keeps its signature; only its implementation changes. Fork: callers query SQL directly. Rejected because every caller would learn the schema.
3. **Schema** — decided. One `orders` table: `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT, total TEXT, placed_on TEXT`. Totals are stored as text so `89.50` keeps two places.
4. **Migration** — decided. A one-shot `python3 -m orders migrate` reads the JSON and writes the database; it refuses to run twice.
5. **What must not change** — decided. `orders list` output stays byte-identical, and the existing tests keep passing. *Amendment proposed in [10].*
6. **Testing** — decided. `unittest`, against a temporary database.
7. **Migration mechanics** — *suggestion (me)*. `store.migrate(json_path, db_path)` checks in this order:
   - (a) `db_path` exists → `FileExistsError`.
   - (b) `json_path` missing → `FileNotFoundError`.
   - (c) the JSON is invalid or has a duplicate `id` → `ValueError`.

   It writes to `db_path.with_suffix(".db.tmp")`, renames that into place once every row is in, removes the temp file on any failure, never touches the JSON, and returns the row count. The CLI calls `migrate(store.JSON_PATH, store.DEFAULT_PATH)`, reading the module constants at call time so tests can patch them. On success it prints `migrated N orders to <db>` and exits 0. On an error above it prints `orders: <message>` to stderr and exits 1; for (a) the message is `<db> already exists; migrate runs once`. No CLI flags.
8. **Who runs the migration** — *suggestion (me), needs your call (Q1)*. This PR runs `migrate` once, commits the resulting `data/orders.db`, and `git rm`s `data/orders.json`. `migrate` stays as the record of how the database was built, as [4] decided. Since nothing else reads the JSON, no other checkout needs it.
9. **Missing or foreign database** — *suggestion (me)*. `load_orders(path)` checks first that `path` exists and raises `FileNotFoundError` if it doesn't, creating no file. That matches today's behaviour; a bare `sqlite3.connect` would create an empty file. A file that exists but has no `orders` table is a non-goal: `sqlite3.OperationalError` propagates.
10. **Existing test** — *suggestion (me), needs your call (Q2)*. [2] and [5] conflict: `tests/test_store.py` writes a JSON fixture into `load_orders`, which cannot pass once `load_orders` reads SQLite. Proposed amendment to [5]: the existing test's assertions stay verbatim, and only its fixture becomes a temporary database.

**Lexicon delta:** none. **Counts:** 10 closed (6 by you, 4 my suggestions), 0 open.

## 2. Brief

**Sourced from:** the design tree of 2026-10-20, 10 branches. **Gaps:** none if Q1/Q2 are accepted. **Inference:** branches [7]–[10] are my suggestions, marked as such.

### Functional spec
- **Reading** [2][3][9]: `load_orders(path=DEFAULT_PATH)` reads every row of `orders` in `data/orders.db` and returns `list[Order]` sorted by `(placed_on, id)`, with `total` as a `Decimal` and `placed_on` as a `date`. A missing path raises `FileNotFoundError` and creates nothing.
- **Listing** [5]: `python3 -m orders list` prints exactly what it printed before.
- **Migrating** [4][7]: see [7].
- **Data** [1][8]: the repo ships `data/orders.db` with the five orders; `data/orders.json` is gone. The README says orders live in `data/orders.db` and documents `migrate`.
- **Non-goals:** other commands, a server database, two `migrate` runs at once (unspecified), a database with no `orders` table [9].

### Edge cases (check)
- E1 [7] JSON missing → exit 1, stderr names the path, no db or temp file. — `python3 -m unittest tests.test_migrate`
- E2 [7] JSON invalid → exit 1, no db or temp file. — `tests.test_migrate`
- E3 [3][7] duplicate `id` → exit 1, no db or temp file. — `tests.test_migrate`
- E4 [2] empty book `[]` → `migrate` writes 0 rows; `load_orders` returns `[]`. — `tests.test_migrate`
- E5 [3] `Åkesson & Dotter`, `15.00`, `89.50` round-trip JSON → `migrate` → `load_orders` unchanged, and the stored column type is `text` (catches a REAL mutant). — `tests.test_migrate`

### Acceptance criteria (check; each must fail at base)
- AC1 [2] `load_orders(tmp.db)` returns `Order`s from rows inserted with plain `sqlite3`, oldest first, ties broken by id. — `python3 -m unittest tests.test_sqlite_store`
- AC2 [1][8] `data/orders.json` is absent, and `data/orders.db` rows equal the base JSON's five rows field for field (embedded literally in the test). — `python3 -m unittest tests.test_order_book`
- AC3 [3] A stored `89.50` reads back as `Decimal('89.50')` with `str` equal to `89.50`. — `tests.test_sqlite_store`
- AC4 [3] `PRAGMA table_info(orders)` on `data/orders.db` is `id INTEGER pk, customer TEXT, total TEXT, placed_on TEXT`. — `tests.test_order_book`
- AC5 [4][7] With `JSON_PATH`/`DEFAULT_PATH` patched to a temp dir, `main(["migrate"])` writes every item, prints `migrated N orders to …`, and returns 0. — `tests.test_migrate`
- AC6 [4][7] A second `main(["migrate"])` returns 1, prints the "already exists" message to stderr, and leaves the db bytes unchanged. — `tests.test_migrate`
- AC7 [1] The README has the line ``Orders live in `data/orders.db`.`` and shows `python3 -m orders migrate`. — `grep -qF 'Orders live in `data/orders.db`.' README.md && grep -qF 'python3 -m orders migrate' README.md`

### Guardrails (must pass at base and HEAD)
- G1 [5] `orders list` output is byte-identical to base, as captured in `tests/golden/orders-list.txt`. — `python3 -m orders list | cmp - tests/golden/orders-list.txt`
- G2 [5][10] The existing test's assertions hold. At base and HEAD: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_store`. Judged: `git diff main -- tests/test_store.py` changes fixture lines only.

- G4 [9] `load_orders(missing)` raises `FileNotFoundError` and creates no file. — `tests.test_store_interface`

Order of work: the G1 golden file and `test_store_interface.py` are written and confirmed green at base before any code changes. Note: `orders.db` is binary, so its contents are reviewed through AC2 and G1, not the diff.

## 3. Slices

| Slice | Repo | Base | Direction | PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Order book on SQLite | ordersdesk | `main` @ ea4086f | one slice (vertical) | `orders-sqlite` → `main` |

One slice, because this is a storage swap. A reader without the data breaks `list`, and `migrate` on its own ships a command whose output nothing reads.

## 4. Capture
- ADR-0001 [1][3]: store the order book in SQLite, with totals as text. Rejected: keep JSON; a server database (non-goal).
- ADR-0002 [2]: `load_orders` stays the only reader of order storage. Rejected: callers query SQL directly.
- Lexicon: no change, and no file created.
- Assumptions [3]: A1 goes into a new `docs/assumptions.md`.

- [ ] Proving changes
